sections.overview: The common earthworm, also called night crawler in North America, is one of the largest earthworms of Europe. It is an epi-anecic species: it lives in a deep, mostly vertical burrow and comes to the surface to feed. It is hermaphroditic, yet each worm still needs a partner to reproduce.
sections.identification: It measures roughly 9 to 30 cm, and the largest individuals are reported at up to 35 cm when stretched in motion. The back is brownish to purplish red and the underside yellow-orange, and the tail end is flattened and paddle-shaped, which lets the worm grip its burrow walls. A German educational reference reports that a mature individual may reach nearly 25 g; mass varies with length and body condition. No sex difference or standard body width was found.
sections.habitat: It prefers undisturbed soil and is common in lawns and grassland. Its permanent burrow normally reaches 1 to 2 m deep, though one source gives up to 2.5 m. On a very thin topsoil over an inert subsoil in north-west England, worms built shallow U-shaped burrows only about 0.11 m deep and still formed a breeding population.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on fallen leaves and other decaying plant material, and takes in soil and plant litter as it digs. It is a detritivore that emerges at night.
sections.behavior: It emerges mostly at night and anchors itself in its burrow with its broadened tail. It builds small turret-like mounds, called middens, at the burrow entrance. Its burrowing is flexible: in shallow soil it adapts the shape of the burrow rather than going down into hostile subsoil.
sections.reproduction: Mating takes place on the surface in wet weather, with two worms lying head to tail, and can last up to four hours. Each worm produces on average about 38 cocoons per year according to one source. Individuals typically mature within a year and may live up to about six years.
sections.ecology: By eating and expelling mineral and organic matter, it aerates and turns over the soil. Densities of 20 to 40 worms per square metre are reported in an average British lawn, and up to 70 per square metre elsewhere, giving this species one of the largest animal biomasses per hectare on land.
sections.conservation: No global conservation assessment was found. In Britain it is described as common and widespread, though badly under-recorded.
